$comment: The maquette's record. Its CSS-EXPORT half was removed on 2026-08-20: `exportedSelectors`, `harnessSelectors`, `probe`, `regions`, `states`, `scope`, `source` and `outOfScope` all served the CSS extraction and its rendering-parity probe, which existed to migrate the app towards the maquette surface by surface. The maquette REPLACES the app (product-intent §15), so there is nothing to export to and nothing to keep in parity with. What remains here is the project's MEMORY — the frozen vocabulary the no-French arm reads, the adversarial review's rules and method lessons, and the reported defects — plus `target`, which `harness/address.py` still reads.

$vocabulary.$comment: The class vocabulary is ENGLISH and FLAT LOWERCASE - `sheetacts`, `herowrap`, `btnprimary`, `screenbar`, `fieldinput`. Measured rather than decreed: of the names this prototype coins for itself none carries a separator, and the only hyphenated ones (`ps-dot*`, `sw-*`) are namespaced imports from elsewhere, where the prefix is what earns the hyphen. A new class takes the flat form.

frenchTokensFrozen.$comment: These allowlisted names read as French and are DELIBERATELY not renamed. They are DATA VALUES that happen to be class-ified - the follow/episode state vocabulary the engine's world data, the `data-ep` state segment and the episode labels all speak - so renaming them moves a CONTRACT, not a stylesheet. They settle when that vocabulary is bound to the backend, never in a naming pass. The allowlist cites this reason rather than merely permitting them. `annonce` belongs to the same family and is listed here too: it carries no underscore, which is the only reason a first pass read it as an ordinary French adjective. It is an EP_LABEL key (« Annoncé »), a rung of the declared lifecycle order and a key of the status-word palette, and it reaches the class attribute the same way its siblings do - by interpolating the episode's state into it.

abbreviationsKept.$comment: Names - short abbreviations and whole words alike - that READ as French at a glance and are KEPT, each decided on evidence rather than on the look of the word. The gate cites these reasons rather than merely permitting the names.
abbreviationsKept.et: The episode TITLE, in the `en` / `et` / `ed` family an episode row draws: episode-number, episode-title, episode-date. All three abbreviations read identically in English and in French, so there is nothing to translate.
abbreviationsKept.pq: The pipeline card's qualifier line (« étape 4 sur 9 · … »), in that card's `ph` / `pt` / `pq` / `pacts` family: pipeline-header, -title, -qualifier, -actions. English once the card itself is `.pipeline`.
abbreviationsKept.vsw: The view switch - a segmented control of icon buttons. An English abbreviation, carried by the design token `--mq-shadow-vsw` as well.
abbreviationsKept.vswwrap: The wrapper the view switch sits in, sharing its English abbreviation.
abbreviationsKept.cadence: An English word, and the engine's own vocabulary for the same idea (`acquire.cadence.*` in the configuration).
abbreviationsKept.r*: The six `r*` spans a list ROW draws: `rt` / `rs` / `rn` inside a topic row (title, subtitle, number) and `rl` / `rf` / `rv` inside a setting row (label, file, value). Every second letter is the ENGLISH initial of what the span holds, and the `r` reads as ROW - which is what both elements are. Their French expansions (rubrique titre, réglage libellé, valeur …) map onto the same six letters, so there is nothing here to translate: the same shape as the `en` / `et` / `ed` episode family.
abbreviationsKept.flux: The list a run's nine steps are told in. KEPT rather than translated, and the reasoning is worth carrying because it is the OPPOSITE of `pilote`'s: `pilote` is spelled the French way and its English cognate means something else (a trial, a first episode), so it genuinely read as French on the page; `flux` is spelled identically in both languages, so a new reader meets an English word rather than a French one. The sense here - the flow of a run, step after step - is looser than the commonest English ones (continuous change, magnetic flux), and that thinness is the whole of the case against it: too thin to justify churn. `flow` is FREE if a future wave touches this family, and the move is cheaper than it looks - the six `f*` children (`fk`, `fn`, `fr`, `fs`, `fw`, `fx`) keep their letters because `flow` also starts with an f, and no production component or hand-written stylesheet names the class at all. Measured footprint: one emission (`<ol class="flux">`), ten declarations, eleven allowlist entries, five selector sites across three rules - and ONE trap, `classList.contains('flux')` in the Système rule, a class name living as a bare string, the shape that has already bitten this vocabulary twice.

$vocabulary.$namesRemoved: `.plein`, `.sansfiche` and `.poster.sansfiche` were dropped from the allowlist rather than translated: the prototype declares no rule for them, emits them nowhere, and the extracted stylesheet has never carried them. They were allowlist entries for classes that no longer exist, and a name nobody can see is not a name to translate.

namesWithKnownAmbiguity.$comment: Names chosen deliberately whose token already means something else somewhere in this prototype. Recorded so the collision stays a KNOWN cost rather than a later surprise.
namesWithKnownAmbiguity.resume: As a CLASS, `.act.resume` is the swipe action that starts searching for a follow again - the pair of `.act.pause`, and the name that replaced `chercher` once `.search` turned out to be the search BAR. As a DATA field, `resume` is something unrelated: a synopsis (`data.ts` declares `resume?: string` and calls it the synopsis; release candidates carry it; the arbitration screen maps it onto `overview`; the arbitration rule reads `.cov` into a key of that name). The two live in different namespaces and never meet, so nothing is broken - but one token now names two unrelated things, and a reader who learns one meaning first will misread the other. `.act.retry` is the alternative if it ever bites.

spreadShapes.$comment: A rename that walks CSS selectors must sweep for the SPREAD operator BEFORE it runs, never after. The last dot of `...name` is not glued to an identifier, so it looks exactly like a selector to any lookbehind written to skip property access - this wave turned `...reglage` into `...setting` and took the whole settings screen down with it (`ReferenceError: setting is not defined`, three rules falling together). The spreads below are live TODAY and their identifiers collide with existing class names, so the next wave touching either name reproduces that defect exactly.
spreadShapes....deck: A live spread over the deck element, and `.deck` is a class.
spreadShapes....port: Live in three places, two of them inside rule code - and `.port` is both a class and a harness selector.
spreadShapes....state: A live spread, and a NEAR miss rather than a collision today: the class is `.states`, not `.state`, so a boundary-anchored rename of `.states` does not reach it. One letter of margin, recorded so nobody spends it by accident.

probe.$comment: THE MEASUREMENT RECIPE, RECOVERED — not rebuilt. Every key below comes from `git show bd31d52b:frontend/maquette/regions.json`, the commit before the untranslate merge (#465) removed this block with the rest of the translation layer. It is recovered rather than re-derived because it is the only replayable measurement recipe this repository ever proved, and rebuilding the list by judgement re-opens a question already settled by measurement (`docs/reference/frontend-architecture.md` § L01). ONE KEY CHANGED, AND ONLY ONE: `allowlist` comes back EMPTY. Its single entry declared `.bottombar` as `position: absolute` in the maquette against `fixed` in the app — a MAQUETTE-VS-APP divergence, which is the model #465 abandoned. This oracle compares the maquette to ITSELF at two commits, so that entry has no subject here, and recovering it would seed the allowlist with a justification for a comparison this instrument never makes. AMENDED 2026-08-20, WITH ITS MEASUREMENT — `computedStyleSubset` goes from 17 properties to 19: `opacity` and `visibility` join it. The recovered list was right for what it used to measure (the maquette against its own extraction, both sides in the SAME interaction state) and is short for what this oracle measures (the maquette against itself at two commits, across 82 states that OPEN AND CLOSE LAYERS). Measured rather than argued: between `lib-list` and `drawer-navigation`, `#scrim` reports all 17 properties identical AND an identical bounding rectangle — only `opacity` and `visibility` move, so the overlay could stop appearing altogether and this instrument would stay green. That is an ADDITION carrying evidence, not the rebuild-by-judgement the lot forbids, and it is flagged to the operator rather than assumed.

knownAbsent.cause: INTERACTION-GATED, not dead: `screens/add.tsx:340` renders it only when `added.size > 0`, and `acq-ajout-resultats` adds nothing. The probe drives states, never interactions, so it cannot reach this without the state declaring the selection.
INTERACTION-GATED: the episode date popover exists in CSS and is mounted by a click. No named state opens it.
WRONG STATE, not dead: `pages/arrivals.tsx:254` renders `.empty` only when the list is empty, and `arr-repos` has arrivals. The region wants a state that empties the list.

neutralise.justification: PROTOTYPE-ONLY CHROME, removed from the DOM before either measurement so both see the same document. The design note is dismissed by a click in a normal harness run, and the rule that keeps it collapsed afterwards lives in BLOCK 2 — correctly NOT exported, since the app never renders a design note. Left in place, swapping the sheet lets it spring back to 75.6px and pushes every region below it down, which the probe would report as a divergence in each one: the shape of a probe measuring its own setup. Removed from BOTH passes rather than allowlisted, because it is not a difference the app can ever have.

regions.$comment: One region per block a user perceives as a unit, anchored on `data-*` and on structural ids — NEVER on a CSS class. The 51 regions this file used to carry were chosen for the CSS-extraction contract and were class-anchored; importing them would break this oracle at the moment it is needed, because L07 replaces those very classes with Tailwind utilities and a region anchored on `.strip` disappears when its surface converts. Filled by phase 2.

More than one buried entry (B-024) walked LATENT, not fixed: the DOM carries exactly five `data-go` producers, four covered by any open layer (page-body content under `#view`), and the fifth — the only one that can ever sit over a layer — allows at most the sheet itself. $adversarialReview.R74: The bridge wires the legacy nav cluster to the router: the shell is the single writer of history entries, speaking through `window.__pont`. The legacy engine keeps its NAVIGATION LOGIC (when to push, when to unwind) and loses only its primitives — it calls the bridge's five verbs (noter, remplacer, coucher, retour, surRetour), implemented on the router's own history instance. The boot order is now INVERTED from what it was: the shell creates the store and the bridge FIRST, and only then calls `window.__startEngine({ magasin })` — the engine's own handshake, called EXACTLY ONCE, after which the engine's boot writes (the arrival state, the guard entry, the back listener) run straight onto the real bridge, in the engine's own order. The envelope's pre-bridge (a queueing `window.__pont` plus a `__rejouerLePont` replay entry point, RETIRED with this change) no longer exists: nothing is recorded and nothing is replayed, so a module that never evaluates simply never calls the handshake, and the startup screen — already first in the frame — stays up rather than covering a half-booted app. Verified by `bridge.py` through six holds: (a) the engine's source holds zero direct history.pushState/replaceState/back/go/forward( — counted after a JavaScript lexer blanks comments and only comments, so that a `//` inside a URL string or a quote inside a regular-expression literal cannot swallow the real calls that follow (measured: the walk preserves the document's 1 897 459 characters and 41 027 lines exactly); (b) the journey (results → sheet → back through the browser's own back) redraws the list and its query through the bridge, and restores its scroll position within R71's own tolerance (the list is scrolled to 300 px before leaving, and the return is asserted within ±40 px — collected and judged, not merely collected); (c) direct entry on ?page=lib&mode=list lands on state.page="lib" and state.libMode="list"; (d) __go on a page-level state does not change history.length; (f′) the handshake is real — `typeof window.__startEngine === "function"` AND `#splash.hidden === true`, measured on a page navigated WITHOUT the harness ever calling `window.__loadingDone` itself (common.ouvrir() calls it to get past the screen; this hold instead navigates directly and reads the screen's own state, so a pass means the INTERFACE hid it, not the harness). The rule itself mutates nothing: the measured copy (/tmp/tm-refonte/wrapped.html, the same bytes the browser is served, never the envelope's source) is shared by every rule of the harness, so a rule that severed it would, on any interruption, fail the NEXT rule for a reason having nothing to do with what that rule holds. Hold (e′) — retiring hold (e)'s two pré-pont halves along with the pré-pont itself — is that a severed module leaves the fail-silent path dead, proven by a mutation applied by hand to the copy, outside any rule, its outcome recorded here: replacing the module script's src (`/vite/index-BzmfI3Gc.js` → a nonexistent file) leaves `#splash.hidden` false and `window.__store` undefined after load, while `window.__startEngine` stays defined (the classic engine script still runs; only the module — which creates the store and calls the handshake — fails to load, two 404s in the console). The startup screen tells the truth instead of covering a broken app. The ritual rebuild restores the copy byte-for-byte (md5 e46876b1fe0c3edce483f21e6982ac52, identical to the pre-mutation copy) and the rule returns green. AMENDED (Task 11): hold (b)'s journey (results → sheet → back) is the R71 journey, and the results screen it walks left `#screen` for a real route (`/add`) the same way R71's own entry describes — hold (b)'s reads follow it to `.screen.open`. STRENGTHENED (ruling R-7, same amendment as R71): `.screen.open` alone cannot distinguish a closed legacy `#screen` from an open one once a migrated screen is also open (DOM order always resolves the React screen first) — hold (b) now ALSO reads `#screen`'s own `open` class explicitly after the back and asserts it false, the fiche this journey opens no longer able to hide behind the React screen's own state. This rule itself still mutates nothing (unchanged principle, see above); the R-7 proof — severing `closeScreen`'s class removal in the shared copy fells this exact same new hold — was run through `screens.py`, which owns the mutation machinery for this journey, and is recorded in full under R71's own amendment; `bridge.py`'s hold (b) exercises the identical mechanism and was re-verified green after the copy's restoration.
$adversarialReview.R79: The library loads more, says when it cannot, and lets one try again. The Médiathèque reads `library.db` locally, so a page of 24 more costs neither quota nor external network: the regime is infinite scroll, and §8 says the count line always tells how many are shown of how many. That left three promises nothing measured, all at the END of the list where only a long scroll reached them — the end of the sample saying it IS the end of the sample and how many titles the prototype really carries (otherwise the last row contradicts the « of 1 861 » counter above it); a failed page saying what remains VALID and offering to try again, the failure being simulated once on purpose because a path nobody can see is a path nobody can judge; and « Réessayer » really loading. The last of those is the ONE control on a migrated page whose handler is a component's own rather than the document-level delegation's, and it is measured with the scroll SENTINEL NEUTRALISED: the sentinel produces the same outcome for a different reason, and that is exactly how a retry that did nothing at all survived being written — its guard read the render's snapshot, where the error it had just cleared was still set. MUTATION: that guard put back, the hold falls alone, naming the count that did not move.
$adversarialReview.R78: Every sort goes BOTH ways, and each way says its own name. The library shipped with three sorts and one direction each — « Ajout récent », « A → Z », « Les plus incomplets » — and asking for the other end of any of them was impossible; the operator reported it (E-001), and an operator who cannot ask for Z → A cannot use a sorted list to find the LAST thing either. The ruling, open to contest: the panel offers the six explicitly, each direction carrying its own NAME rather than an arrow bolted onto a shared one — « Ajout récent » reversed is « Ajout ancien », « Les plus incomplets » reversed is « Les plus complets », which is what one would say out loud. The alternative, tapping the already-chosen sort to flip it, costs half the rows and is INVISIBLE: nothing on a phone says that a second tap on the row one just chose does something else, and a row reading « A → Z » that answers Z → A is the opposite of showing what the machine will do. The direction rides beside `data-settri` as `data-reversed`, so the attribute that was already a contract keeps its meaning. Reversing is a SECOND PASS and never a second comparator, because « ajout récent » has no comparator at all — its order is the source's — so one `.reverse()` at the end says the same thing for all three. THE REVERSAL IS MEASURED ON WHAT IS DRAWN, on a library narrowed until the whole set fits on one page: the list draws its first 24 of 260, so reversing the order and taking the first page again gives the LAST rows of the other end — right, and not the reverse of what was drawn. A first version read the rows through `data-mediasheet` and measured nothing at one end of the library, where no title resolves to an embedded sheet: the title every row draws is the identity, the sheet is a property of some rows. MUTATION: the direction stops being applied, in the served copy alone — the three reversal holds fall, each naming its sort, while every hold about the NAMES stays green, which is the whole point: a page that says « Z → A » over a list in A → Z passes everything except this.
$adversarialReview.$comment: Every reported defect was generalised into a RULE checked across all states (harness/audit.py and audit2.py), not fixed on the reported case alone. The implementer inherits the rules, not the anecdotes. AMENDED (SP4b, the media sheet moves to the shell): the per-state sweeps resolve their ROOT through a ladder (`#dlg` → `#screen` → `#sheet` → the page), and the media sheet left `#screen` for a real route (`/mediasheet/$title`, rendered inside `#coquille`). The fiche now joins that ladder in `audit.py`, `dest.py` and `states.py`, named by the identity it carries — `.screen.open[data-cle^="fiche:"]` — and placed LAST, so every pre-existing case resolves exactly as before and a dialog or a panel opened OVER the fiche is still what gets measured. Without it the five `fiche-*` states fell through to `#view`: the rules did not fail, they measured the page UNDERNEATH and passed on it — the failure mode this file exists to make impossible. The gap was visible in the numbers, once looked at: the three `fiche-serie` / `fiche-film` / `fiche-sans-trailer` states reported the SAME 1541 characters and 3 skeletons, which is the library page behind them; each now reports its own media (2136 / 953 / 1787 characters, no skeleton). AMENDED (SP4c, the ladder generalises): the per-identity fiche:/ajout: pair at the ladder's tail — repeated verbatim in every sweep that needed it — is replaced by ONE generic rung, `.screen.open[data-cle]`, still LAST after the legacy `#dlg`/`#screen`/`#sheet` trio. Any screen migrated off `#screen` onto a real route answers to it by construction, without naming its prefix: the fiche and the add screen it used to spell out, the arbitration screen and the release picker this wave (SP4c) moves onto routes, and `ProfileScreen` — migrated in an earlier task but never added to this specific ladder pair, a hole this generic rung closes as a side effect rather than a fourth case to remember by hand. `audit.py`, `dest.py` and `states.py` carry the change; `audit2.py`'s R11 ladder and `audit.py`'s own R8 `couches` list follow the same move, each recorded under its own entry below. Measured on `states.py`: `arr-resolution` read `couche:false, txt:1944` before (the acquisition page underneath) and `couche:true, txt:1520` after (the arbitration screen itself); `ecran-releases` read `couche:false, txt:2348` before and `couche:true, txt:1022` after — the SP4b proof shape, on the two newest routes. AMENDED (the code speaks English): the harness scripts were renamed to English FILE NAMES by the wave that puts the source in English — twenty-seven Python scripts (panneau→panel, coquille→shell, ecrans→screens, adresses_ecrans→screen_addresses, commun→common, serveur→server, and so on) plus the renommer→rename Node script. Every rule↔file pointer in this file names the new script. The entries below stay keyed by R-NUMBER, which is what a rule is identified by: a file name says where a rule LIVES and is never the rule's identity, so only prose mentions moved — no rule's assertions, holds or counts changed, and the full suite is green from the new names.
$adversarialReview.R1: Every tappable poster leads to a FILLED-IN sheet (synopsis, genres, cast). Otherwise the poster is not a button.
$adversarialReview.R2: A button must have a declared DESTINATION, not merely a known class. A real href counts as a destination. $adversarialReview.R3: Touch target >= 32px. DECLARED EXCEPTION: the episode cell is 31 × 27 in the shipped component — at 13 per row, 44px would demand 572px. A geometric constraint, not an oversight.
$adversarialReview.R4: No horizontal overflow outside declared scrollers (.pillscroll, .cast, .eps). An element clipped by an ancestor does not count, provided the clipping ancestor itself fits; the scrollport must also offer no real horizontal scrolling. AMENDED (SP4b): `states.py` measures the fiche itself rather than the page behind it — a screen whose overflow was never checked was passing this rule on someone else's geometry. AMENDED (SP4b fix-wave, the add-media screen joins the ladder): `/add` left `#screen` for a route the same way, and every state opening it was, until now, measured on the library page underneath — its overflow joins the fiche's rung, named by its own key (`.screen.open[data-cle^="ajout:"]`). AMENDED (SP4c, the ladder generalises): `states.py`'s fiche/ajout pair is replaced by the ONE generic rung described in the `$adversarialReview` root comment — the arbitration screen and the release picker join by construction, with no third prefix to add by hand.
$adversarialReview.R5: A horizontal scroller NEVER sets touch-action: pan-x alone — it would block vertical panning.
$adversarialReview.R6: No essential title is truncated (.ht, .sheettitle, dialog title).

The export allowlist had drifted to 107 classes out of 237: more than half the CSS would never have reached the app. harness/export.py classifies every class by what it actually does and fails on anything uncovered or dead.
Slicing the stylesheet on the string « BLOCK 2 » cuts the header comment's opener and leaves an orphan closer: the header's own prose then parses as selectors. Slice from the comment opener.

Sampling a fixed handful of states hides whole families. R13 sampled five frozen states, none of them an incomplete medium — which is exactly where a divergence went unseen. Draw the sample from the DATA.

A geometric measurement taken before the layout has settled is worthless in BOTH directions. Measuring at 110 ms reported three states as overflowing; at 400 ms the same states are clean — and the same margin can hide a real overflow behind a green. Rules that read boxes wait 300 ms; rules that read a rendering choice do not need to, and R30's verdict was verified identical at 35, 200 and 450 ms rather than assumed.

An adversarial probe is as capable of being wrong as the thing it probes. A first pass accused the light theme and narrow viewports; both were artefacts of the probe — a stale open layer counted as content, and a settle time too short. Isolate the variable before reporting a defect, or the review costs more than it finds.

Three adversarial passes on new angles found nothing in the prototype and three faults in the probes themselves: a stale open layer counted as content, a settle time too short, a « Tout » pill summed alongside the parts it totals, and an undo tested by bypassing the function that creates the undo. A probe is as capable of being wrong as the thing it probes — isolate the variable and re-measure before reporting, or the review costs more than it finds. What the passes DID find was one real defect, and it was found by asking a question no existing rule asked.

SIXTEEN of nineteen harness scripts could not fail: they computed their verdict, printed it, and exited zero. Any orchestration would have seen them all green regardless. Wiring each verdict to its exit code immediately surfaced a test that had been broken and silent — it waited on a selector the library stopped using once its cards led to the media sheet. A script that cannot fail is not a test; it is a report nobody is obliged to read.

A gesture proven only under synthetic touch is a gesture proven on half the sessions. Testing with a real mouse on a browser with no touch at all found two defects a thumb would never meet: the browser's native image drag eating the pointer stream after two moves, and a release outside the frame never reaching a listener bound to the scrollport.

The prototype draws a phone inside a wide page, so the app's breakpoints — which measure the WINDOW, correctly, because in the app the window IS the phone — switched the frame's contents to the desktop presentation on a desktop screen: the bottom bar vanished from something 390px wide. The frame re-asserts the mobile values, in the harness block, because the app rule is right. It must be revisited whenever a breakpoint is added: a rule that only holds for the breakpoints that existed when it was written rots quietly.

An action drawn on ONE surface is an action the interface does not really have. « Compléter » existed only as a button on a card, so the poster view of the same list could not complete anything. R43, the rule written for it, found the identical hole in « Récupérer » and « Résoudre » the first time it ran — neither had been reported.

Two builders for one object drift apart in silence. A medium had a rich panel from a card and a thin one from a gallery, and neither carried every action. Deriving ONE panel from what is true about the medium — followed, incomplete, in the library, blocked — makes the two paths equal by construction rather than by vigilance.

A rule can encode the workaround instead of the concern. R31 forbade library cards from opening the acquisition sheet, because that sheet offered follow actions to media nobody followed. Fixing the cause made the rule fail on correct code. Rewrite such a rule onto what it protects.

A failing check must still REPORT. Breaking R41 on purpose made the run crash inside R43 on a null it no longer guarded: the exit code was right and the output was a stack trace. A rule whose failure buries the other findings is half a rule.

Uniformity is measurable: breaking the shared card builder on purpose now produces 332 failures across every list, where the same edit once reached only the lists that happened to use it. Three views rebuilt a card by hand, and one of them had already drifted.

« One component with variable display » fails when the variation is named after appearance. The card takes a DESCRIPTOR of facts — fraction, chip, caption, fresh — and a view that wants something not in it must add the fact, never pass ready-made markup. An envelope guarantees nothing about what it carries.

Not everything that looks like a card is one. The release candidate shares the markup and is a different object: no sheet, no panel. Forcing it into the shared component would have made it promise both. It is marked instead, so the contract check tells them apart by construction rather than by knowing which screens draw which.

A shared component is worth what its LAST holdout is worth. Découvrir kept its own builder and its own class vocabulary, and drew a poster 63 % larger than every other list — on a page that already offers two visual formats for browsing. Measuring geometry across the five list surfaces found it in one pass; reading the code had not.

« The data already contains markup » is not a reason to accept markup. The suggestion reasons shipped their own <b>, so the card would have had to trust them. Converting the data to segments — plain text plus what is emphasised, at its position — keeps the escape total and emphasises the right « 4 », which re-matching a string into a sentence does not.

A screen extracted from its context loses what it INHERITED there. The login gate came out of the prototype without the reset that surrounds it: the wordmark fell back to Times, and `max-width: 340px` applied to a content box instead of a border box, so the card rendered 378px wide. Worse, the title was black on black — legible-looking in the DOM, invisible on screen. Extraction must carry the inherited foundations, or restate them.

A media query asks the wrong question for a component. It reads the viewport, so a 390px frame sitting on a 1280px desktop is told it has room for six columns it does not have — which is why a harness deviation had to pin three columns by hand. A container query asks the width actually available, and the app gets the same answer because there the scrollport IS the window; the deviation could then be deleted.

Deleting a CSS rule by its selector destroys the rule when that selector is LAST in a group. Removing `.sugtile img` took the whole `user-drag: none` block with it and left `.swipe img, .sugwrap img, .deck img, .tile img,` dangling. Native picture drag came back and swallowed the pointer stream — one down, two moves, never an up — and three gesture tests failed for a reason that looked nothing like a CSS deletion.

Renaming an attribute must check the name is FREE. `data-sugwrap` was renamed to `data-dismiss`, which already existed as the control that dismisses a suggestion: a tap on a poster then read as a press on that control and threw the suggestion away. The element removed and the control that removes it are two things and need two words.
The harness serves a COPY. Editing the prototype and running the suite without re-syncing measures the previous version, and the report looks like a fix that did not take.

A service worker on a design reference must not cache. Its only job is to make the page installable — a caching worker would serve yesterday's prototype to someone judging today's design, which is the one failure a reference cannot afford.

Renaming identifiers needs a PARSER, not a regex. The same short name is declared in many scopes with many meanings — `t` was a title, a trimmed query and a touch point — so a global replace preserves behaviour while lying about meaning. And a hand-rolled tokenizer desynchronises in the 14 MB of embedded base64: one attempt renamed 715 occurrences and silently missed posterBox, leaving the file half-renamed. Scope analysis gives the exact range of every reference, and touches nothing else.

Shorthand object syntax makes an identifier its own property KEY. Renaming the `n` in `{ n, aired, own }` renamed the key too, and every reader of `.n` downstream got undefined — sheets fell back to a list rendering. The rename must expand to `n: number` instead.

A collision check must read the FINAL names, not the original ones. Outer scopes are renamed first, so by the time an inner scope is examined its parent may already hold the name about to be chosen: `const el` and a nested `const f` both became `element`, legal to the parser and a temporal dead zone at runtime.

A derivation that sizes something against a population that thing already SETS reads back its own answer. The list poster was derived from the median card's height, and the size it produced now floors 113 of the 192 cards drawn — so the median card IS the poster, and re-running the derivation cannot move it. Two more things the re-measurement showed: the arithmetic as written dropped the card's 1px borders, which made it a RATCHET adding 1.33px on every application rather than a fixed point; and the population is bimodal — 13 of 18 lists draw a median card of 115.9px while five long lists of compact rows drag the global median to 83 — so the median over all cards and the median over lists disagree by 52 %, and no derivation lands between them. A derivation must be run on a population the derived value does not itself produce, and a median over a bimodal population answers a question nobody asked.

A named state must PIN everything a later reading is taken from, and the loudest of those is the data scenario. `__reset` restored the world and the filters but not `scen`, so a state that switched to the dense scenario left it switched for the next one: the same surface answered differently measured on its own and measured after its neighbour. It hid a mutation test — the rule under test passed because the state it ran on was not the state it was written against. The scenario now returns to rest with everything else.

A long press and a drag are opposite cases for the compositor, and one rule cannot serve both. It claims a DRAG on the first move and fires `pointercancel` straight away, which kills a gesture that was never going to be a scroll — so the pull to refresh reads the touch stream and ignores the cancel. It claims a PRESS only once the finger has really travelled, so there the same `pointercancel` is the honest signal that it became a scroll. Measured, and the measurement also showed why the tolerance has to live on the pointer stream: Chrome delivers NO `touchmove` at all for a drift of a few pixels, only `pointermove`, so a tolerance written on touch events would never run. And a probe that drifts by one pixel proves nothing — the browser suppresses it, so the mutation test passed against a tolerance of zero.

A named state must name ALL its dials, not only the ones it means to exercise. `state.pipe` was left unnamed by the Arrivées states that do not care about the pipeline, so the same id rendered differently depending on which state had been visited before it — and the parity probe's whole premise is that it does not. R10 found it. That is the exact cost of state nobody owns, and it is the third axis's second question showing up as a defect rather than as an opinion. The mirror of it: a rule's snapshot must carry every dial the interface tracks, or an action that moves one the snapshot forgot reads as inert — R10 accused « Lancer le pipeline » of doing nothing, and a false accusation costs as much as a missed defect.

Assert the property that was PROMISED, not a symptom of it. « No panel appeared » is not « the click was swallowed »: the first passes whenever the release happens to land off the card, and it certified an unswallowed click through four attempts to reproduce the defect it was hiding. When a rule states a mechanism, measure the mechanism — `defaultPrevented` here — rather than the consequence one hopes it has.

Compare a rendering against the DATA it claims to show, never against the wording. A check that matched a scheduler's sentence with a pattern failed on « le 9 août » — a perfectly healthy row — because it was measuring its own pattern rather than the interface. Reading the declared field off the page and comparing the rendered colour to it is exact, non-circular, and proves the one thing worth proving: that the derivation was not bypassed by a value written in by hand.

A tone has TWO jobs — a fill and a label — and one colour cannot do both. `--danger` is painted behind white text on a button, so it sits at a lightness that reads THERE; used as the label colour on a 20 % tint of itself it landed at 3.69, under AA. Nobody had noticed because the defect only shows once the tone is used as text, and it was worse in the light theme — success at 2.91, warning at 2.02, on every chip in the interface, for as long as chips had existed. Measure a colour in BOTH themes or half the design is uncertified.

The VOCABULARY belongs to the rule, not to the data. Comparing a rendered tone against the declared one proves the renderer follows the data and nothing else: mutate the data and both move together, so colouring a nearly-full disk as a critical alert changed nothing and the check stayed green. That is a derivation reading back its own output — the same shape that once sized a poster against itself. The mapping from a WORD to the tone it deserves is stated in the rule instead, once, and a disagreement is a defect whichever side wandered.

PM2's counters mean three different things depending on what they count, and none of them is « how unhealthy is this ». On a DAEMON, `restart_time` counts manual restarts — the design host sits at 92 because the procedure asks for one after every edit to `serve.py`, and its unstable count is zero. On a SCHEDULED JOB the same field counts RUNS, which is why the hourly health check reads 263. And `unstable_restarts` — PM2's own word for « died before min_uptime » — is not a crash on a scheduled job either: a job that finishes and exits has, by definition, died before min_uptime. Two of these were printed raw on screen as though they were facts one reads. A figure whose meaning changes with the row is a figure the operator has to decode, which is the opposite of what a line is for — and it was found by being asked « où veux-tu en venir ? » about a number nobody had checked.
